# Pair Notebook

Most assignments ask you to hand in code. This one asks you to hand in **the
conversation you had while learning something**.

A Pair Notebook is one module of this course taught as a one-on-one tutoring
session. You talk to an AI tutor in your **terminal**. Beside it, in your
**browser**, a [marimo](https://marimo.io) notebook fills up as you go —
figures, sliders you can turn, photographs of your own pen-and-paper work, and
notes that quote your answers word for word.

At the end you have a notebook that is your own illustrated lecture note. That
notebook is what gets graded.

::: {.callout-tip title="What is graded"}
**Your thinking, not your code.** No programming experience is required.

Needing hints is **not** penalized. The session log is read for *how you
reasoned* — asking questions and taking detours counts in your favor. That is
the whole point of the exercise.
:::

A session takes about 60–90 minutes. You can stop anywhere and pick it up later.

## A session, start to finish

Here is what the two windows do. Use ◀ ▶ to step through it yourself.

{{< include _pair-notebook-walkthrough.qmd >}}

## Before your first session

About ten minutes, once per machine. Everything after this is just `pi`.

### 1. Open a terminal

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### macOS

Press `⌘` + `Space`, type **Terminal**, hit enter. That is all you need — the
shell it opens is `zsh`, which is what the instructions below assume.

#### Windows

Install [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win) first. You need it
to hand your work in, and `pi` uses the bash it brings.

You then have two ways to open a terminal, and **both work**:

- **Git Bash** — Start menu → type **Git Bash**. The commands on this page work
  as written, and your home folder is `/c/Users/<you>`.
- **Windows Terminal** or **PowerShell** — Start menu → type **Terminal**. Same
  commands, except for the one place noted below where PowerShell spells things
  differently (setting your key).

If you have no preference, use **Git Bash**: everything in this course is
written for it.

:::

### 2. Install Node.js and uv

|                                                                   | what it is                | Windows                            | macOS              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 24+                                 | your tutor runs on it     | `winget install OpenJS.NodeJS`     | `brew install node` |
| [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/)     | runs the notebook         | `winget install astral-sh.uv`      | `brew install uv`   |

Close the terminal and open a new one afterwards, so the new commands are found.
Check with:

```bash
node --version   # v24.x or newer
uv --version
```

### 3. Put your API key in your shell profile

Your instructor issues you a key that looks like `sk-nsci-…`. It is how your
tutor reaches the course models.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### macOS / Git Bash

Add this line to `~/.zshrc` (macOS) or `~/.bashrc` (Git Bash), then open a
**new** terminal so it takes effect:

```bash
export NETSCI_API_KEY="sk-nsci-..."
```

#### PowerShell

Run this once — it stores the variable for future sessions:

```powershell
setx NETSCI_API_KEY "sk-nsci-..."
```

Then close the window and open a **new** one. To check that it took:

```powershell
echo $env:NETSCI_API_KEY
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Never put the key in a file in your assignment folder"}
You hand this assignment in by pushing that folder to GitHub. A key committed
there is a key that has to be revoked and reissued. Keeping it in your shell
profile keeps it out of your repository.
:::

Your key has a weekly allowance. <https://llm.skojaku.com/v1/usage> tells you
what is left of it.

### 4. Get your assignment folder

Accept the assignment link on **GitHub Classroom**. It creates a repository for
you. Clone it and go into it — this is the folder you will run everything in:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/sk-classroom/advnetsci-pair-notebook-m02-small-world-<your-github-id>
cd advnetsci-pair-notebook-m02-small-world-<your-github-id>
```

### 5. Run the setup script

Inside that folder:

```bash
node setup-pi.mjs
```

It is the same command on Windows and macOS. It installs `pi` (the agent your
tutor runs on), registers the course models in `~/.pi/agent/models.json`, and
makes **one real request** so you find out here — not mid-lesson — whether your
key works. It is safe to re-run, it backs up any `models.json` you already had,
and it leaves your other providers alone.

When it prints `You are set`, you are done.

### 6. The tutor's toolkit installs itself

You do not install it by hand. The folder's `.pi/settings.json` pins the two
packages your tutor needs, and `pi` fetches them the first time you run:

```json
"packages": [
  "git:github.com/sk-classroom/pi-pair-notebook@v0.3.0",
  "npm:@juicesharp/rpiv-ask-user-question@2.4.0"
]
```

That first start therefore takes a few seconds longer than every one after it.

<details>
<summary>If the fetch fails and you want to install them by hand</summary>

```bash
pi install git:github.com/sk-classroom/pi-pair-notebook@v0.3.0
pi install npm:@juicesharp/rpiv-ask-user-question@2.4.0
pi list     # both should be listed
```

Use the **same version tags** as the folder — a module and its toolkit are
tested together.

</details>

## Starting a session

Inside your assignment folder, type:

```bash
pi
```

That is the whole command. **There is no slash command to start** — say hello in
plain words and your tutor takes it from there. It starts the notebook itself,
opens it in your browser, and shuts it down again when you are done.

::: {.callout-note title="Have pen and paper ready"}
Three steps happen off-screen, on real paper — a table, a drawing, a
derivation. You photograph each with your phone and drop it into the notebook.
:::

## The two windows

| Window                    | What it is                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Terminal** (tutor)      | Where you and your tutor talk. Every question and every answer happens here.                                                          |
| **Browser** (notebook)    | The whiteboard: figures, interactive experiments, and photo uploads. It is built one cell at a time as you go.                        |

Three things in the notebook are worth knowing about:

**📨 Send to my tutor.** A drop box or a code box has this button under it.
Press it and your tutor sees your work. A slider or a radio button has no
button — play with it, then just say what you saw in the terminal.

**📷 Photo uploads.** Photograph your paper with your phone, drop the image into
the box, and press send. Your tutor reads the photograph. Wonky handwriting is
fine; it is your reasoning that is being read.

**⚖️ Stuck with your tutor?** Always the last thing on the page. If you think an
answer should have counted, you want a fresh try, or you would rather move on —
say so there and press the button. A second, stronger model reviews the whole
situation and makes a call your tutor has to follow. Using it is never held
against you.

## Handing it in

You do not upload anything by hand. When you are done for the day, tell your
tutor in the terminal:

> `hand it in`

It commits your notebook, your session log and the summary, and pushes them to
your GitHub Classroom repository. Three files land there:

| File                                       | What it is                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| `notebook.py`                              | the notebook the two of you built       |
| `session_artifacts/session_log.jsonl`      | your answers, verbatim                  |
| `session_artifacts/session_summary.md`     | a summary for your instructor           |

Stopping halfway and picking it up tomorrow is fine — hand it in each time you
stop. **A session finished in three sittings is worth exactly as much as one
finished in a single evening**, and the commit history simply shows when the
work happened.

<details>
<summary>Doing it yourself instead</summary>

```bash
git add -A && git commit -m "Pair Notebook 02" && git push
```

</details>

## If something goes wrong

**`pi: command not found`** — re-run `node setup-pi.mjs`, then open a new
terminal. The install puts `pi` on your `PATH`, and an already-open terminal
does not see it.

**The notebook did not open in your browser** — tell your tutor. It has the
address and will hand it to you.

**Your tutor stops mid-sentence, or a request fails** — check your allowance at
<https://llm.skojaku.com/v1/usage>. If there is plenty left, quit with
`Ctrl` + `C` and run `pi` again; the session picks up where it left off.

**Anything else** — ask on Discord. Getting stuck on setup is not part of the
assignment.
